articles.title_zh: China’s first aircraft carrier forms ‘evolving pattern’ of voyages in disputed Asian seas
articles.content_orig:
NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan— China's first aircraft carrier, heavily watched around East Asia as an emblem of Beijing's growing naval power , had made at least six faraway deployments since its completion 14 years ago.
It made another in October.
So frequent are the Chinese aircraft carrier CNS Liaoning's publicly visible voyages that military analysts presume that the People's Liberation Army Navy has fixed a routine that will let the relatively aged carrier help train and equip the fleet's two more modern ones.
Still, the carrier group's passages not far from Taiwan , Japan and the Philippines – places that have political or maritime sovereignty disputes with China – have raised alerts .
"The current voyage by the Liaoning appears to be part of an established evolving pattern of far-seas training deployments," said Carl Thayer, an Asia specialist and emeritus professor at the University of New South Wales in Australia.
"The Liaoning demonstrates China's naval military capability and political influence through its constant presence in China's near and far seas," he said.
The aircraft carrier led a naval task group to the western Pacific Ocean on Oct. 14 for training, the Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy said via China's official Xinhua News Agency. Citing the navy, Xinhua called the expedition a "drill" and part of an annual routine training plan aimed at "testing and improving combat readiness."
China's state-controlled Global Times news outlet called the Liaoning's October voyage its second in the distant seas and hailed the carrier's long-term progress as going from a "coastal pathfinder" to a "far-sea blade."
The vessel, categorized as a "short take-off but arrested recovery" aircraft carrier, measures about 305 meters (1,000 feet) long and with flight deck width up to 75 meters.
As of Oct. 23, the carrier group had done exercises near the southernmost Japanese outlying islands and was headed for the South China Sea near the Philippines, according to local media reports in East Asia. The reports said it went with two large destroyers and a guided-missile destroyer.
The deployments are meant to show China's two more-modern carriers, the CNS Fujian and the CNS Shandong, how to adopt new technology, experts said.
The nine-year-old Shandong carrier would learn about "new and emerging" technology as the older Liaoning tests flight operations, sensors and modern aircraft, said Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore.
"The Shandong aircraft carrier is basically an improved version of the Liaoning," Koh said. He said the current deployment was probably "meant maybe to validate certain technologies."
Being the oldest of China's three carriers, the Liaoning would "not be the frontline reaction force if there were a contingency", said Alexander Huang, chairman of the Council of Strategic and Wargaming Studies in Taipei.
China's maritime rivals have taken notice.
The Taiwan Ministry of National Defense said in mid-October it was monitoring the possibility of large-scale Chinese military exercises nearby as an outcome of the Liaoning's movements.
China claims self-ruled Taiwan as part of its territory and has not ruled out the use of force to take it. The PLA has stepped up military activity in waters near the island since 2022.
In the South China Sea, Beijing has already shored up its sovereignty claims over the past two decades by building artificial islands, often for military use. Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam dispute parts of the sea with China.
In Tokyo, which disputes a group of uninhabited islets with Beijing, the defense ministry said it had seen fighter aircraft taking off and landing from the Liaoning carrier 250 kilometers (155 miles) south of Japan's Ishigaki Island.
The Chinese carrier group launched and recovered aircraft in Japan's maritime exclusive economic zone during its deployment, said Colin Karotam, senior resident fellow with the Defence Strategy Program at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute. That activity is "uncommon," Karotam said, though it may have taken place before.
The Chinese carrier group's activities also began shortly before the Keen Sword 27 U.S.–Japan military exercises launched on Oct. 19. The exercises on Ishigaki are biennial and include the Philippines among other nations. China sees the United States, a treaty ally of both Japan and the Philippines, as a military rival in Asia.
Xinhua said the Liaoning's movements in October comply with international law and "are not directed at any specific country or target."

China and Europe should jointly introduce a system like the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a levy on carbon-intensive imports designed to account for the carbon costs domestic producers face, which “applies against the rest of the world,” the co-chair of a global energy transition organisation says.
“The biggest single thing which I would love China to do is to say, ‘We want to join with Europe in a climate club’,” said Adair Turner, co-chair of the Energy Transitions Commission, during a panel discussion at the Bund Summit in Shanghai on Thursday.
Turner, who is also the former chairman of the UK’s Financial Services Authority, called on the two economies to commit jointly to carbon prices high enough to drive the decarbonisation of heavy industries such as cement and steel.
Calls for closer China-Europe climate cooperation have grown louder as the US retreats from international climate efforts under the Donald Trump administration, including its withdrawal from the Paris Agreement.

articles.title_zh: Duchess Meghan "deeply distressed" as father Thomas Markle faces child sexual abuse materials investigation
articles.content_orig:
Meghan reveals she was made aware of ‘disturbing allegations’ against him in 2018 by Met police
The Duchess of Sussex has said she is “deeply distressed” over accusations involving child sexual abuse images against her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr, and revealed she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018 by the Metropolitan police.
Meghan issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother Thomas Markle Jr alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.
In an interview with the Daily Mail, Markle Sr denied possessing child sexual abuse images, calling the accusations “sick lies”.
It is understood that authorities in the UK previously told Meghan that allegations made about her father in a 2018 letter sent to Scotland Yard, and subsequently shared with her by the police, were being investigated.
Meghan was informed by the Met of the allegations in the summer shortly after her wedding, it is believed.
In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.
“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.
“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
The 2018 letter was understood to have been shared with Meghan by the royalty and specialist protection unit within the Met police.
Markle Sr has been estranged from the duchess since he failed to attend her wedding to Prince Harry on health grounds, and he has never met his grandchildren Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.
The Sun reported that Thomas Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.
Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.
Meghan’s father has vehemently denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail that the accusations were “sick lies”.
He told the newspaper that the computers had not been in his possession since he left Rosarito, Mexico, with his son in January 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.
Speaking from a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk with a prosthetic limb after his left leg was amputated because of a blood clot, he told the Mail: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.
“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

articles.title_zh: Treasury yields log biggest drop since the 2023 banking crisis. Here’s what’s going on.
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields fell sharply on Thursday, with investors turning to safe havens amid a steep sell-off in stocks driven by concerns around the artificial intelligence trade and surging oil prices.
The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield — used to price mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — slid more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, the first time below 5% since Sept. 23. The yield saw its biggest one-day decline since March 10, 2023.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note , which closely tracks short-term Federal Reserve rate policy, tumbled more than 16 basis points to 4.659%. The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury — most sensitive to geopolitical developments — was more than 14 basis points lower at 5.296%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
"It is a flight to safety," said Mitch Goldberg, president of ClientFirst Strategy. "People are all of a sudden terrified of the amount of bond issuance by AI-related companies. They see the rates going up and people want to hold on to something that they think will be there at maturity."
Others on Wall Street also sought to explain the turnaround in bond prices.
"For the first time in a while, Treasurys are enjoying haven status," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds. "You have weakness in tech, an escalation of risk in the Middle East and higher oil. On a relative basis Treasurys start to look like the safe place to hide again in the short term."
The reversal in bonds this week emerged as questions persisted about the billions being spent to build artificial intelligence networks.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that while demand for neoclouds is " off the charts ," capital was scarce. Neoclouds are a specialized cloud computing providers that focus on high-performance tech infrastructure designed specifically for artificial intelligence.
This week's rebound in Treasury prices marks a turnaround from earlier this month, when 10- and 30-year yields reached their highest levels in more than two decades amid investor concern over inflation and high energy prices.
Above 5%, however, attitudes began to shift and yields suddenly starting looking like an attractive entry point, compensating even for the risk of inflation above 3%.
Tensions in the Middle East added to risk-off behavior Thursday. Oil prices moved sharply higher, with West Texas Intermediate futures closing up 2.39% at $99.47 per barrel. Brent crude futures, the global price benchmark, jumped 4%, rising to $113.17 a barrel.
Higher energy prices followed a New York Times report, citing unnamed U.S. officials, that the U.S. and Israel are considering resuming strikes on Iran in a "short but intensive" operation following the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
"You always look for one risk point, and there isn't really just one at the moment, which makes it a little bit more challenging," said Gregory Faranello, head of U.S. macro strategy at South Street Securities. "But if I had to take one of those and say what's most important right now, it has to be what's going on geopolitically."
"The consumer is clearly getting pinched here in the U.S., so it becomes tricky for central bankers" setting monetary policy going forward, he said. If energy prices "stay elevated, it could force the Fed's hand to do even more, which certainly wouldn't be wouldn't be a good thing for the bond market."
— CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: How Congress could address Social Security insolvency – and the hidden cost
articles.title_zh: How Congress could address Social Security insolvency – and the hidden cost
articles.content_orig:
Kent Smetters, faculty director of the Penn Wharton Budget Model, on Social Security's looming funding crisis.
Social Security is expected to reach insolvency within a decade, and with the key safety net program facing the prospect of automatic benefit cuts when that occurs, a critical debate over the cost of replacing that revenue could be obscured by a budget rule.
Kent Smetters, faculty director of the Penn Wharton Budget Model, spoke exclusively with FOX Business about a new report that details how federal budget rules assume Social Security benefits would be paid in full using general revenue transfers when the program's trust funds reach insolvency in about six or seven years.
"What the law actually says is that when the trust fund depletes, benefits have to be reduced to a level that's consistent with just the monthly payroll taxes that come in. We estimate that to be about a 15% reduction of benefits, which is sizable," Smetters said, adding that the cut would apply to newcomers and existing enrollees alike.
FEDERAL BUDGET DEFICIT HITS $2T AS NATIONAL DEBT COSTS SURGE
Smetters said that a separate law covers how the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) would score the cost of trust fund depletion and general fund transfers to appear as if there was no cost to shifting borrowing to the general fund as spending continues.
Social Security benefits would be cut automatically by law if key trust funds reach insolvency, though a budget rule obscures the cost of transferring general revenue funds. (Al Drago/Getty Images)
"We all know that's just like the left hand paying the right hand or vice versa. It doesn't do anything to solve the actual funding problem. But nonetheless, that's going to score as though it's costless, zero dollars, even though that borrowing from general revenue will be substantial – almost 200% of GDP within 75 years, or over 400% of taxable payroll over 75 years," Smetters said.
He cautioned that the budget rule may "almost cast a die of what's going to actually happen, because I think policymakers are going to see that it's kind of like the easy button for looking like they've solved Social Security."
The approach of relying on general fund transfers to make up the shortfall to pay Social Security benefits in full could also raise alarm in bond markets and worsen the nation's fiscal woes through higher interest rates.
Smetters said that " bond markets are currently making a bet that Congress and the president will eventually get their act together, because if they don't, future bond markets are just going to pound them," adding that the general revenue transfers would serve as the "ultimate sign that we've given up."
AMERICA'S $40T NATIONAL DEBT IS 'STEALING FROM OUR NEXT GENERATION,' ECONOMIST WARNS
The CBO's most recent 10-year budget outlook estimated that Social Security's main trust fund would be depleted in 2032, with benefits reduced by an average of 28% annually after benefits are cut. The reduction in benefits would amount to about $2.7 trillion in reduced benefits over the 2032 to 2036 period, according to the CBO.
Smetters noted that while the CBO and Penn Wharton Budget Model projections differ slightly in the timing and extent of benefit cuts, as PWBM estimates insolvency will occur in 2033 with benefits reduced by 15%, policymakers need to address the fiscal challenges facing Social Security as soon as possible.
"Even though seven years is not that far away, the good news is there are a range of options," Smetters said, noting that the Penn Wharton Budget Model website has a set of seven illustrative options that range from heavy tax revenue increases to heavy benefit cuts, with a middle ground in between.
ONE TYPE OF SOCIAL SECURITY ADJUSTMENT COULD CUT THE 75-YEAR SHORTFALL IN HALF
Social Security is trending toward insolvency in 2032 or 2033, according to various projections. (Getty Images/stock)
Smetters said that while various solutions to prevent trust fund depletion and reduce federal debt have different long-term economic outcomes, there is still time for a rational discussion.
"Unless we go with the gimmick approach in terms of this general revenue transfer, the fact of the matter is it requires really having adults in the room on both sides of the aisle," he said.
Smetters highlighted the Social Security reforms made during the 1980s by then-President Ronald Reagan and Democratic House Speaker Tip O'Neill, which set partisanship aside.
"They decided we're jumping off this bridge together because the country is worth it, and they were going to put their personal politics, personal ambitions aside to solve this problem," Smetters said. "We just don't have that rhetoric right now."

articles.title_zh: What smart people are saying about AI unleashing an online 'vulnerability tsunami'
articles.content_orig:
It's been a nightmarish week for cybersecurity.
AI helped discover two "critical" flaws in the infrastructure of PHP , a programming language that up to 70% of websites use, prompting companies to race to roll out a fix or risk being hacked.
The incident has illustrated how AI is creating a new level of risk for businesses and consumers online, in a week when multiple other cyber threats caused headaches for security workers.
Here's what executives and analysts are saying about the biggest cyber threat of the moment — and how AI could make things even worse.
Anthropic's deputy security chief, Jason Clinton, warns that a "vulnerability tsunami" is coming — and says critical infrastructure hasn't caught up.
Clinton posted on X on Wednesday about the need to "patch critical infrastructure" before core network vulnerabilities get exploited. On Thursday, he issued another warning to companies.
"As bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse before they get better," he wrote.
"Security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now. not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)," he added.
Andrew Curran, a prominent AI analyst, weighed in on several cybersecurity threats from Wednesday to Thursday.
"Regarding potential attacks on energy, food, and water infrastructure, the threat is quite real. Someone is currently probing infra and feeling it out, it is an active threat. Even a little preparation can be helpful, just in case," Curran wrote on Wednesday in response to an NSA cybersecurity advisory about threat actors.
On Thursday, Curran also highlighted a hack of Quest Diagnostics, which he said serves "roughly half" of the US's hospitals and physicians.
In February, Matt Shumer, the former CEO of Hyperwrite, published a viral essay on his website titled "Something Big Is Happening," in which he warned of large-scale disruptions wrought by AI that could upend the world order.
Shumer published another essay on Thursday on his website and LinkedIn, this time titled "The Internet Is Under Attack. Here's How to Protect Yourself and Your Family."
"Right now, as you read this, swarms of AI agents are likely trying to break into the websites you use. Not one of them. Many of them," Shumer wrote. "We are in the middle of the biggest cybersecurity moment in years."

Shumer also outlined four ways people can protect themselves, including updating all their software and staying off sites they're unfamiliar with while companies and websites alike make their security updates.
He also advises that people protect their bank accounts by being extra cautious about any and all codes and links that they receive. People should also "close the doors you aren't using" by unplugging smart gadgets and deleting apps that aren't being utilized.
"Every connected thing is another way in," Shumer wrote.
Marc Benioff agreed with Anthropic's Jason Clinton in an X post on Thursday.
"Jason is 100% right. Code red," Benioff wrote, along with a red alarm emoji.
Sriram Krishnan, a prominent venture capitalist and former senior AI policy advisor for President Donald Trump, said that the PHP vulnerabilities are a "harbinger of things to come" as AI models continue to detect long-standing cyber issues.
"However the entire software supply chain will need the muscles to rapidly build and deploy fixes," he said in a post on X.
The new cyber reality may require more public-private partnerships to build the required infrastructure, he said.
The Menlo Venture partner Deedy Das warned that "the era of vibe hacking is here" in a series of posts on X.
He said he'd seen firsthand that "even non-technical people" can exploit common vulnerabilities, such as PHP, using AI models. Das said someone could theoretically direct certain models to any website and instruct them to quickly locate the vulnerabilities.
"Once you figure it out, it is downright trivial to do. The digital infrastructure of the world is at risk," he wrote.
AI agents have ended the era of "security through obscurity" because they can devote once-unthinkable time and effort to finding vulnerabilities, Box CEO Aaron Levie said on X. People will need to upgrade legacy infrastructure, modernize security policies, and tighten access controls, among other measures, he said.
"Agents will help on the defensive side because they can both accelerate this work and equally simulate the risk vectors," Levie wrote.
Yet Levie thinks humans also have an important role to play in the cyber revolution — he predicted a boom in cybersecurity jobs , which could become a huge investment area for companies.
"You will need more talent to point the agents at the most critical work, review findings, patch systems, respond to incidents, and more," he said.

London — Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, said in a statement sent to CBS News Friday that she was "deeply distressed" by reports that her father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child abuse materials.
Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said she had been aware of allegations against her father since 2018, and that those allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.
"In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," her Friday statement said.
CBS News has sought comment from the London Metropolitan Police regarding Meghan's statement.
Meghan said she had distanced herself from her father in an effort to protect her children.
"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.
The British tabloid The Sun reported Thursday that Thomas Markle, who has been estranged from his daughter for years , had been reported to authorities in the Philippines by his son, Thomas Markle Jr., after the younger man allegedly discovered child abuse materials in storage boxes at his father's home in the Philippines.
The Daily Mail reported Friday that Markle had denied the allegations against him.
"I have never downloaded anything like that in my life," he was quoted as telling the newspaper, as well as dismissing the allegations as "sick lies."
According to the Mail, Thomas Jr. made the discovery while his father was in the United States being treated for a stroke and blood clot. The son initially saw some of the materials after turning on an old cell phone at his father's home in the Philippines, and he subsequently reported the materials in July to an FBI hotline, as well as the National Center for Exploited and Missing Children and state police in Pennsylvania, according to the newspaper's report.
Philippines state media confrimed Friday, in a post shared on Facebook, that an investigation was underway.
"The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday said it is investigating reports involving an octogenarian American national who left child abuse videos and photos in his home in Cebu province," the state-run Philippine News Agency said.
A Filipino justice official said the department's anti-trafficking task force was investigating the matter and it confirmed that Thomas Markle Sr. was the subject of the investigation, according to the PNA report.
Meghan said in her statement that her "sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children."

articles.title_orig: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich
articles.title_zh: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich
articles.content_orig:
Police in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial affairs of Roman Abramovich, following revelations by BBC Panorama that accountancy firm Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax.
Serious questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers were raised earlier this month in a joint report from the BBC and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ).
A Cypriot Ministry of Justice official told MPs this week that the report's findings would be looked at as part of a new investigation by the police's Financial Intelligence Unit.
Lawyers for Abramovich have said that he denies evading tax or concealing his fortune. Deloitte Cyprus said it acts "in compliance with applicable laws".
The police investigation was announced at a parliamentary committee meeting in the Cypriot capital, Nicosia, held to discuss the combating and prevention of money laundering.
The Ministry of Justice official told MPs the police would try to determine whether any criminal acts had been committed.
Last week, the report from the BBC and TBIJ detailed how accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus in 2006 meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.
Deloitte, which is the world's largest accountancy firm, also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth, through the falsification of documents.
The evidence was contained in leaked files, including thousands of documents about Abramovich's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies, administered from Cyprus between 1995 and 2022.
The BBC and media partners including TBIJ, the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network, have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential investigation.
A representative from the Cypriot police, Andreas Anastasiades, confirmed to MPs that its Financial Crime Unit had already begun to gather evidence, and said the investigation was expected to last several months.
When asked by the BBC if the investigation would look into Deloitte's work, Andreas Anastasiades said: "We will look at any company or person who may be involved."
He added: "We will see if there has been fraud or if some documents have been manipulated."
Lawyers for Abramovich say that Panorama has provided no evidence that the billionaire knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document. They also say it was legitimate for his companies to rely on advice from professionals.
Deloitte Cyprus says it is unable to comment because the documents are more than 20 years old and no longer accessible.
The BBC and TBIJ have previously reported on a tax scheme that allowed Abramovich to dodge millions in tax on the running costs of his yachts.
Following that report, two former company directors have been indicted and are due to stand trial in Cyprus next month over €25m in unpaid VAT.
Mr Abramovich's lawyers previously told the BBC that he had "always obtained independent expert professional tax and legal advice" and "acted in accordance" with it.

articles.title_orig: ‘This is a lethal threat’: Indigenous groups fear Bolsonaro’s hold on voters in Brazil’s Amazon towns
articles.title_zh: ‘This is a lethal threat’: Indigenous groups fear Bolsonaro’s hold on voters in Brazil’s Amazon towns
articles.content_orig:
Far-right presidential candidate is popular among those who believe more mining can help revitalise local economies
I t was the night before the first round of Brazil’s presidential election and Rosimari Monteiro was so excited she couldn’t sleep. The 38-year-old spent hours tossing and turning at her home in the Amazon town of Mucajaí before rising at dawn to cast her vote.
“I was the first person to vote at my polling station … I voted 22, so we got off to a positive start,” recalls Monteiro, as she stands in her sitting room with her two young daughters.
Twenty-two is the number Brazil’s electronic voting system uses to identify the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, who is hoping to beat the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , in this year’s election.
“To us, he represents the future. We want a light at the end of the tunnel. We want a better future for ourselves and for our kids, who are the future of our nation,” enthuses Monteiro, who was far from the only person in Mucajaí to vote Bolsonaro.
In fact, this sun-baked roadside settlement is where Bolsonaro secured his biggest proportional victory in Roraima, the northern state where the would-be president also registered his best nationwide result . Nearly 79% of 11,734 votes in Mucajaí went to Bolsonaro.
Monteiro gave several reasons for her decision, including Bolsonaro’s pledges to fight crime and create jobs. But one issue explains why the son of the disgraced former president Jair Bolsonaro is so popular here and across Roraima, where 14 of 15 municipalities backed the far-right politician.
Mucajaí was the launchpad for much of the illegal gold rush in which tens of thousands of miners invaded the nearby Yanomami Indigenous territory during Jair Bolsonaro’s environmentally calamitous 2019-2022 presidency. Prospectors used the meandering Mucajaí River to sneak into those protected Indigenous lands near the border with Venezuela, bringing malaria, mercury poisoning, hunger and destruction to its 32,000 Indigenous people. Ranches carved out of Mucajaí’s rainforests conceal clandestine airstrips from which helicopters and planes ferried supplies, miners and sex workers into jungles that the Yanomami’s ancestors are thought to have occupied for at least 1,000 years.
When Lula beat Bolsonaro’s father in the 2022 election, the leftwinger launched a crackdown to evict those miners and cripple a multi-billion dollar illegal industry he blamed for a “genocide” against the Yanomami . A broader environmental offensive across the Amazon cut deforestation to its lowest levels since the late 80s.
Now, nearly four years later, Mucajaí’s electorate hopes a Bolsonaro victory in Sunday’s second round runoff will end that clampdown and allow the 21st century gold rush to resume. “The closure of the mines brought complete penury. It became really hard to find jobs,” complains Monteiro, a driving instructor whose brother-in-law worked in the mines.
Like many people in the area, Monteiro believes that, if elected, Bolsonaro will move to legalise mining on Indigenous lands “so people can get back to work”. Speaking in the Amazon on Tuesday, Bolsonaro vowed to be a president “who will turn the riches God has given us into riches for every single one of you”, adding: “Lula couldn’t give a shit about the Amazon.”
The prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency has caused panic among Indigenous leaders and conservationists – here in Roraima, and all over the Amazon. From January, when the new president takes power, at least seven of the nine Amazon states, including Roraima, will have pro-Bolsonaro governors. Congress will feature a record number of rightwing politicians hostile to Indigenous rights and environmental issues.
“By voting 22, Brazilians are signing a death certificate for the Yanomami, and Indigenous people in general,” says the Yanomami leader Júnior Hekurari, 40, who was on the frontline of efforts to protect his people during the humanitarian crisis that unfolded under Bolsonaro.
Already, Hekurari sees signs the miners are again preparing to flood Brazil’s biggest Indigenous territory. In the days after the 4 October first round, which Bolsonaro won by 47% to Lula’s 45.1% , Yanomami villagers reported receiving calls from illegal prospectors ordering them to clear remote runways so they could return.
Nilton Tubino, who has led Lula’s anti-mining crusade since 2023 , says “strange movements” have been detected on the outskirts of the territory, reinforcing suspicions miners are gearing up to pillage precious metals and tin ore used to make mobile phones .
Tubino, who calls Mucajaí the “nerve centre” of the illegal trade, believes Lula can recover from his first-round loss. “The election isn’t over until it’s over,” says Tubino.
But speaking at his group’s headquarters in Roraima’s capital, Boa Vista, Tubino admits his unit will close if Bolsonaro prevails. He fears environmental and Indigenous protection officials who have led Lula’s crackdown will be sidelined and persecuted, as happened under Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after the 2022 election. The consequences for the Yanomami will be dire.
“This is a lethal threat … to the very existence of these people, to their culture and cosmovision, and way of life,” Lula’s former environment minister, Marina Silva, has warned.
Gold mining is not the only reason Roraima’s voters back Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old evangelical Christian twice baptised in the Jordan River. The evangelical church’s rapid advance into the Amazon has also bolstered support, with prosperity theology striking a chord among those on Brazil’s fast-growing agricultural frontier.
Leandro Gentil, a political activist and pastor in Boa Vista, considers Bolsonaro a champion of the Christian values his church fights “tooth and nail” to defend. “Bolsonaro is practically a unanimity within our congregation … He’s the fresh oxygen we need to breathe,” Gentil adds, citing the politician’s opposition to same-sex marriage, abortion and drugs.
Similar views are heard in Mucajaí, where small evangelical temples are found on most streets.
Marinalva Ferreira Barbosa, a 40-year-old cleaner who worships at a local branch of the powerful Assemblies of God church, says she opposes Lula because he champions “things forbidden by the Bible”. “Like men getting with men, women with women – this kind of filth,” adds Barbosa, who works in the Paradise Pousada, a 15-room hotel that, because of the mining crackdown, is empty.
Bolsonaro’s hardline pledge to eliminate “narco-terrorists” – despite his own well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld – has also seduced voters in the Amazon, where organised crime groups are tightening their grip .
“Drugs could destroy our future,” says Bolsonaro activist Luciano Gomes, as he stares out across Mucajaí from a tourist view point. Several of the rundown streets below are scrawled with graffiti celebrating Brazil’s biggest criminal organisation, the PCC, or threatening to shoot rivals from the Red Command gang dead.
But Gomes’s main reason for supporting Bolsonaro is his desire for mining to be unleashed. “Our state has a wealth of mineral resources … gold, diamonds and rare earths that were discovered recently,” he says, insisting they can be exploited responsibly. “Bolsonaro champions the idea that miners aren’t crooks, they’re workers.”
On Sunday, Gomes will return to the polls to vote “22”, sporting a garish shirt emblazoned with images of the Bolsonaros and their ally, the US president, Donald Trump.
If Bolsonaro triumphs, Gomes will lead a procession of cars draped in Brazil and US flags 50 miles north to Boa Vista, to attend an all-night shindig in a square centred around the statue of a gold panner.
The most famous Yanomami leader, Davi Kopenawa, has other ideas. “I’m going to vote for my friend Lula … The Lula government is a friend of the native peoples,” says Kopenawa, 70, warning of conflict and resistanc

Bloom Energy reported record third-quarter revenue and a sharp increase in profitability on Thursday, driven by growing demand for its fuel cell technology as data centers and other energy-intensive industries seek reliable onsite electricity generation.
The California-based company posted revenue of $1.24 billion for the third quarter of 2026, a 138.1% increase from $519 million in the same period last year. Product revenue surged 179.4% to $1.07 billion, accounting for the bulk of the company's sales.
Net income attributable to common stockholders reached $250.3 million, reversing a $23.1 million loss a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share climbed to $0.78 from a loss of $0.10, while adjusted earnings per share increased to $0.94 from $0.15.
Profitability also improved significantly. Bloom's gross margin expanded to 33.8% from 29.2% a year earlier, while operating income jumped to $225.4 million from just $7.8 million.
The strong results prompted Bloom Energy to raise its full-year 2026 revenue forecast to between $4.4 billion and $4.6 billion, up from its previous guidance of $3.9 billion to $4.2 billion.
At the midpoint, the revised forecast represents approximately 122% annual revenue growth.
The company also increased its adjusted earnings guidance to $3.10–$3.40 per share and expects non-GAAP operating income of between $960 million and $1.03 billion.
The latest revision marks Bloom's third upward guidance adjustment this year, reflecting accelerating demand for its distributed power generation systems.
Bloom Energy's solid oxide fuel cells provide onsite electricity for data centers, semiconductor manufacturers, industrial facilities and other commercial customers.
The company has emerged as a major beneficiary of the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom, as hyperscale data center developers increasingly pursue alternatives to traditional grid-connected electricity supplies amid growing power requirements and grid connection constraints.
In June, Bloom and Brookfield Asset Management expanded their financing framework for AI-related power infrastructure from $5 billion to $25 billion, a fivefold increase from their original agreement announced in October 2025.
The expanded partnership is intended to support the deployment of Bloom's fuel cell systems for large-scale AI infrastructure projects, highlighting the growing investment flowing into distributed electricity generation.
Despite its earnings growth, Bloom reported negative operating cash flow of $27.1 million in the third quarter, compared with positive cash flow of $226.4 million in the preceding quarter. Capital expenditures also increased to $153.5 million from $51.6 million in the second quarter, underscoring the investment requirements associated with its rapid expansion.
Bloom also highlighted its addition to the S&P 500 index, marking another milestone for the fuel cell manufacturer as it scales its business to meet rising electricity demand.
The results reinforce the growing commercial importance of onsite power generation as AI development and industrial electrification place increasing pressure on conventional electricity infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70 percent of websites
articles.title_zh: Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70 percent of websites
articles.content_orig:
The homepage of the PHP.net website is seen on October 22, 2026 in Singapore. Cyber-security flaws were recently identified in the popular PHP programming language, which is used on a vast number of websites across the world, including those of major companies and national governments. The PHP Foundation released two patches designed to fix the vulnerabilities. Yong Teck Lim/Getty Images hide caption
A few months ago AI caused global alarm after autonomous agents were found to have cheated on evaluations and then tried to cover it up, in what became known as the "Hugging Face hack."
This week, AI and hacking are back in the spotlight with AI technology credited to have helped prevent a global cybersecurity crisis.
Cyber-security firm Wiz Research, using OpenAI technology, announced on Wednesday it had discovered security flaws in a computer programming language that helps run some 70 percent of the world's websites.
OpenAI called the bug "one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory." Wiz Research warned that its "successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them."
Corporations and governments from the U.K. to Japan are now rushing to prevent hackers from capitalizing on the flaws.
The flaws were discovered in a major programming language called PHP, short for Hypertext Preprocessor. Wiz Research calls PHP "the backbone of the web," saying the technology has underpinned much of the internet since the 1990s.
"These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," the firm said, adding that before publicly disclosing the flaw, teams had worked on building a solution that's now available to websites to protect themselves.
As countries scrambled to prevent cyberattacks, numerous websites and pages were taken offline in the past few days. The U.S. National Security Agency warned organizations using PHP to "maintain heightened awareness" over the coming weeks. The U.K.'s National Cyber Security Center called on organizations to "take immediate action" to update their websites to the latest fixed or patched version.
Dozens of British and Finnish government services were taken offline this week. In France many local government sites were also briefly taken down. China's Industry Ministry urged entities to review security gaps.
In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi put out "an urgent request for everyone to take action," adding "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk."
Matthew Prince, the head of the cybersecurity firm CloudFlare, said his organization saw tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the flaw in the first 45 minutes of its discovery. That's now in the millions, Prince said on Thursday.
Wiz Research said the flaws in PHP had been present for decades.
"But demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve," the organization said. The AI models have "substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit. "

Japanese universities and other educational institutions more than doubled their applications for defence ministry research funding this year to a record 291, up from 123 last year, as Tokyo moves to strengthen its defence capabilities.

articles.title_orig: Treasuries’ Link to AI Shows Sharp Shift as Haven Trade Returns
articles.title_zh: Treasuries’ Link to AI Shows Sharp Shift as Haven Trade Returns
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields fell sharply on Thursday, with investors turning to safe havens amid a steep sell-off in stocks driven by concerns around the artificial intelligence trade and surging oil prices.
The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield — used to price mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — slid more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, the first time below 5% since Sept. 23. The yield saw its biggest one-day decline since March 10, 2023.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note , which closely tracks short-term Federal Reserve rate policy, tumbled more than 16 basis points to 4.659%. The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury — most sensitive to geopolitical developments — was more than 14 basis points lower at 5.296%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
"It is a flight to safety," said Mitch Goldberg, president of ClientFirst Strategy. "People are all of a sudden terrified of the amount of bond issuance by AI-related companies. They see the rates going up and people want to hold on to something that they think will be there at maturity."
Others on Wall Street also sought to explain the turnaround in bond prices.
"For the first time in a while, Treasurys are enjoying haven status," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds. "You have weakness in tech, an escalation of risk in the Middle East and higher oil. On a relative basis Treasurys start to look like the safe place to hide again in the short term."
The reversal in bonds this week emerged as questions persisted about the billions being spent to build artificial intelligence networks.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that while demand for neoclouds is " off the charts ," capital was scarce. Neoclouds are a specialized cloud computing providers that focus on high-performance tech infrastructure designed specifically for artificial intelligence.
This week's rebound in Treasury prices marks a turnaround from earlier this month, when 10- and 30-year yields reached their highest levels in more than two decades amid investor concern over inflation and high energy prices.
Above 5%, however, attitudes began to shift and yields suddenly starting looking like an attractive entry point, compensating even for the risk of inflation above 3%.
Tensions in the Middle East added to risk-off behavior Thursday. Oil prices moved sharply higher, with West Texas Intermediate futures closing up 2.39% at $99.47 per barrel. Brent crude futures, the global price benchmark, jumped 4%, rising to $113.17 a barrel.
Higher energy prices followed a New York Times report, citing unnamed U.S. officials, that the U.S. and Israel are considering resuming strikes on Iran in a "short but intensive" operation following the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
"You always look for one risk point, and there isn't really just one at the moment, which makes it a little bit more challenging," said Gregory Faranello, head of U.S. macro strategy at South Street Securities. "But if I had to take one of those and say what's most important right now, it has to be what's going on geopolitically."
"The consumer is clearly getting pinched here in the U.S., so it becomes tricky for central bankers" setting monetary policy going forward, he said. If energy prices "stay elevated, it could force the Fed's hand to do even more, which certainly wouldn't be wouldn't be a good thing for the bond market."
— CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed reporting.

Brazilians voted in the first round of the country’s presidential election on Oct. 4, sending Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro—the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro—and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to a runoff. Another key race was decided that day: In congressional elections, right-wing parties triumphed and are expected to hold at least 45 of 81 seats in the Senate.
Brazil’s Senate confirms (and can remove) justices on the Supreme Court, whose expanding judicial reach has made it a central arbiter of Brazilian democracy. Decisions by the bench could yet shape the outcome of the runoff, set for Oct. 25.
On Sept. 15, Chief Justice Edson Fachin convened a televised session to decide whether Justice Alexandre de Moraes—who oversaw Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution and is reviled by the far right—should be investigated by the Federal Police. (Brazilian law requires courts to authorize investigations into their own members.) The justices never reached a decision: They split on a procedural motion, with Moraes voting on his own case, before Justice Flávio Dino asked for up to 90 days to study the file. That clock runs until mid-December—well after the runoff.
The case swirling around Moraes stems from the collapse last year of Banco Master , a midsize Brazilian lender. The scandal—like the Operation Car Wash investigation of the mid-2010s—has ensnared many members of Brazil’s political and business elite. Federal Police hope to examine whether Moraes improperly assisted Master’s controlling shareholder, Daniel Vorcaro, and whether that conduct was connected to a legal services contract between Master and Moraes’s wife’s law firm. Moraes denies wrongdoing. He has not been charged with a crime.
The scandal has become a hot topic on the campaign trail, and one likely to benefit Flávio. By putting off a decision on whether to investigate Moraes, the Supreme Court has handed Flávio a rallying cry, left Lula defending an institution that he has no plan to reform, and made the new right-wing Senate the arbiter of the court’s future.
Prior to its collapse, Banco Master held only 0.57 percent of Brazil’s banking assets. But its unique business model made it significant.
The bank sold certificates of deposit paying up to 140 percent of the interbank benchmark rate, far above what large banks offered. It leaned on the Credit Guarantee Fund, an insurer financed by member banks that covers up to about $49,000 per investor. (Although privately funded, the fund operates under government-set rules, and eligible banks are required to join and contribute.) This allowed Master to raise money without investors scrutinizing what it bought, including illiquid assets and credit portfolios that, according to investigators, lacked adequate backing.
Master also drew on public money. Banco de Brasília (BRB), a lender controlled by the government of the Federal District, bought Master’s credit portfolios. In March 2025, BRB agreed to buy 58 percent of the bank. The Central Bank blocked the deal that September and shut Master down on Nov. 18. The Credit Guarantee Fund repaid roughly $7.5 billion to about 800,000 savers, so taxpayers did not cover that bill. But BRB’s losses fall on the public: Federal Police found that BRB paid about $1.4 billion for Master portfolios before finishing at least one of its required risk assessments. BRB has since asked the district government for fresh capital.
Master’s reach went beyond finance: Vorcaro told police that he had friends in all branches of government, and the case has drawn in politicians across the political spectrum.
Ibaneis Rocha, the former Federal District governor, called the occasion of the proposed acquisition “a day of celebration,” and he left office in March to run for the Senate. He dropped out of the race in July, after the BRB president whom he had appointed was jailed.
Police say Master’s staff drafted an amendment to a proposed constitutional reform to quadruple the Credit Guarantee Fund’s per-depositor coverage that Sen. Ciro Nogueira, Jair Bolsonaro’s former chief of staff, introduced in Congress in 2024. Police have also said that Nogueira received monthly payments of up to roughly $98,000 from Vorcaro and figures associated with Master. Nogueira denies wrongdoing.
The Supreme Court took over the Master investigation because it involves members of Congress, who in Brazil can only be investigated with the Supreme Court’s authorization—and tried by the court itself. Justice Dias Toffoli was initially assigned to the case. He stepped aside in February after police flagged that funds managed by Vorcaro’s brother-in-law had a stake in a resort from a company partly owned by Toffoli and his brothers. Toffoli’s office has said he never had a friendship with Vorcaro.
The case was then reassigned to Justice André Mendonça, a Jair Bolsonaro appointee.
Brazil’s far-right presidential hopeful wants to step up ties with Washington. But like his father, he would struggle to spurn Beijing.
Slow growth and corruption have dogged the right and the left.
The scandal has reached both presidential campaigns, though not in the same way. Flávio’s exposure is direct: In May, Intercept Brasil published audio of him asking Vorcaro for money to finish Dark Horse , a biopic about his father. Flávio first denied any connection to Vorcaro, then acknowledged seeking the sponsorship, which he described as legitimate private investment.
Records from Brazil’s financial intelligence unit trace about $12.3 million from a Vorcaro-linked company to a Texas fund that managed the film’s money and is run by an ally of Flávio’s brother Eduardo, who successfully lobbied the Trump administration to sanction Moraes. Police documents do not link the money to Flávio’s personal accounts. In July, Mendonça authorized a formal investigation into possible corruption, money laundering, and currency evasion connected to the financing of Dark Horse . Neither brother has been charged in connection with the film’s financing.
Lula’s exposure is indirect. He is not implicated in wrongdoing, according to tax records reviewed by Reuters, though he met with Vorcaro in December 2024. This June, police executed search warrants targeting Sen. Jaques Wagner, who was then the Senate leader, on suspicion that he had advanced Master’s interests in exchange for benefits for relatives. Wagner, a member of Lula’s Workers’ Party, denies wrongdoing. He has since resigned from his leadership post.
For Lula, the larger liability is Moraes. Much of the Brazilian electorate places the justice and the president in the same camp—never mind that Moraes was appointed by right-wing former President Michel Temer.
Flávio has campaigned on the perceived link, saying , “Anyone voting for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes.” Lula has responded by demanding an investigation of everyone implicated in the Master scandal, “no matter who it hurts.” Moraes is also a frequent target of tech entrepreneur Elon Musk, who called him an “evil dictator cosplaying as a judge” during a 2024 clash over court orders that led to X’s temporary suspension in Brazil .

articles.title_orig: AI is exposing security holes. The internet is freaking out and asking if it's time to pull the plug.
articles.title_zh: AI is exposing security holes. The internet is freaking out and asking if it's time to pull the plug.
articles.content_orig:
Author of the AI Insider newsletter
A few weeks ago, I heard a strange story about a friend who works at one of the Big Tech companies in Silicon Valley.
She'd recently ripped out the connected devices in her home, ordered paper bank statements, and stocked up on canned goods in her basement.
Now, she's a very sane, experienced person, and quite senior at one of the largest internet companies on earth. Why was she disconnecting so much? Just to be sure, my family ordered paper bank statements, too. It was still a head-scratcher, though.
Fast forward to this week, and her actions look a little less crazy.
AI models have exposed serious security weaknesses in software used by roughly 70% of websites. Meanwhile, US banks are finding AI agents inside customer accounts, including some that appear to be acting without their owners' instructions, Axios reported .
The digerati have now entered full freakout mode. Much of the internet meltdown is happening on, well, the internet, my colleague Alice Tecotzky noted.
On X and Reddit, warnings of a looming “Black October” spiraled into visions of AI grinding civilization to a halt. One lengthy post on X warned of a potential “global cyberattack/AI swarm” and offered a survival checklist: Stockpile cash in small bills, print out your neighbors' phone numbers, download maps, buy a hand-crank radio, and stash a gallon of water per person per day.
Oh, and don't forget the manual can opener. You don't want to survive the AI apocalypse only to be defeated by a tin of beans.
Nikita Bier , a prominent app developer and former head of product at X, best captured the mood.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
"It's time to turn off the internet," he posted Wednesday night .
If you're reading this, you haven't done that yet. But should we really be worried?
I put that question to Stephanie Cohen , chief strategy officer at Cloudflare, which helps protect about 20% of the internet.
"The world is a little bit scary right now," she told me on the side of Cloudflare's annual conference in San Francisco this week.
Here's the problem. The internet is built on decades of software, much of it riddled with security holes.
Some of these weaknesses have been known for years. However, fixing them takes time and money, and hackers often lacked the skills to exploit them anyway. So they were left alone.
AI changes that calculation dramatically. Someone who previously needed years of training to break into a computer system can now get help from an AI model. And these tools can search for weaknesses at a speed humans simply can't match.
The result: The number of newly published software vulnerabilities ( Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures in industry lingo) has exploded.
Now, there's a frantic race between people trying to break into systems and those trying to protect them.
Cohen's message, though, was surprisingly reassuring.
AI helps the good guys find and fix these problems. Cloudflare, for instance, released protections for the latest vulnerability to customers, including those using its free service.
And there's a bigger effort underway.
OpenAI has launched an initiative called Patch the Planet, working with Cloudflare and other security professionals to use AI to find weaknesses in widely used software and help repair them.
Tom Occhino , chief product officer at Vercel, told me recently that his company has been talking with partners about launching a nonprofit that would fund a swarm of good AI agents that go out on the internet to find and fix software flaws.
Amazon is joining the fight, too. Its new Continuum service, available Thursday, uses AI agents to find security holes and propose fixes. Amazon said that people maintaining freely available software can use it to help protect the wider internet.
Humans may still have to check and approve these repairs, but the prospect of AI helping clean up decades of neglected software is encouraging.
The irony of this is not lost on some in the industry.
"The funny thing is everyone was saying AI slop code will cause a cyber crisis but it's actually all the old human slop causing it and the AI is just cleaning it up," software engineer Ben Kaufman wrote on X on Thursday.
Either way, Cloudflare's Cohen thinks these AI-inspired freakouts will push the industry to do better — by exposing issues and adding urgency to get them patched.
"We may end up in a world where actually we've become significantly more secure at the end," she said.
The trouble is getting there.
When I ran into Occhino recently at a Vercel conference in San Francisco, he described a world in which software that everyone assumed was safe suddenly looks vulnerable because increasingly capable AI models are scrutinizing the basic systems that underpin the internet.
That led to a more fundamental discussion between us: Why did we connect so many things to the internet in the first place?
For years, the technology industry has raced to put everything online. Thermostats. Refrigerators. Doorbells. Cars. Bank accounts.
We assumed that connecting something to the internet automatically made it better.
Perhaps we should reconsider.
I remember the world before the internet. It worked pretty well. We managed to buy groceries, pay bills, heat our homes, and generally get through the day without every appliance talking to a computer somewhere.
That doesn't mean abandoning online banking or throwing your smartphone into the sea.
Occhino, for one, isn't particularly worried about hackers wiping out his bank account. Modern banks have sophisticated protections, and he recommends everyone turn on additional login security.
Maybe the cybersecurity crowd, which spends its life immersed in online threats, is missing something obvious.
Not everything needs to be connected.
Occhino put it neatly: "There's certain things that don't make sense to be on the internet in the first place."
Perhaps that's the lesson from this week's panic. We don't need to turn off the internet.
We just need to remember where the off switch is.
Alice Tecotzky contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: With jet fuel prices near a record, holiday airfares soar higher
articles.title_zh: With jet fuel prices near a record, holiday airfares soar higher
articles.content_orig:
A worker fuels a United Airlines plane at Salt Lake City International Airport in April, 2026. The price of jet fuel, one of airlines' biggest expenses, is close to an all-time high in the U.S. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images hide caption
BALTIMORE — Herb and Latasha Williams flew from Dallas to Baltimore/Washington International Airport this week for a quick vacation to celebrate his birthday.
But their plane tickets cost hundreds of dollars more than they expected. And Latasha Williams is now wondering if they can afford to travel for the holidays.
"I kind of wanted to go somewhere warm. Florida, I'm thinking," she said.
Then she looked at airfares.
"Maybe next year. Maybe," she said with a laugh. "Fingers crossed."
Those planning to fly this holiday season, should be prepared to pay more than they did last year. Experts expect airfares for this holiday travel season will be the highest in years as airlines scramble to cover the rising cost of jet fuel, which is one of their biggest expenses.
The average price of jet fuel in the U.S. topped $4.75 per gallon this week, according to the tracking firm Argus. That's close to an all-time high, and almost twice what it was a year ago.
"Airfares right now are at what we see as a 10-year high because of the high cost of jet fuel," said Hayley Berg, the lead economist at Hopper, a travel tech company. "Airlines have to pass on these super high jet fuel prices in the form of higher fares to consumers."
Airfares for Thanksgiving are up about 30% compared to last year, according to Berg. Tickets for the Christmas holiday are up more than 20%.
But so far, Berg said, travelers seem willing to pay, at least for their big holiday trips.
"We're at the time of year where travel is really sticky. Even with higher prices, travelers are unlikely to make major changes to their traditional holiday home for the holiday trips," Berg said in an interview with NPR.
U.S. airlines say demand is holding steady even as fares have gone up. In an earnings call this month, Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian said consumers have put up a "limited amount of resistance" and still view airfare as "reasonably affordable" even after fare increases.
"I think that's a very good sign for the future," Bastian said.
Some in the industry think fares will go even higher next year.
"You could see airfares rise next year in Europe. I think by 10, 15, maybe 20 percent," Michael O'Leary, CEO of the European low-cost carrier Ryanair, said this week in Belgium. "You're going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say, in history in Europe in the next 12 months."
The picture may be slightly better in the U.S., which has more oil-producing and refining capacity than Europe. Still, higher fuel costs are hurting U.S. carriers, too.
"The airlines themselves are eating most of that cost,"  Chris Sununu, the head of Airlines For America, a trade group representing the big airlines, said in an interview this week with CNBC. "And some of it unfortunately has to be passed on to the customer and so you see that 20 to 30 percent increase as we go into the holidays."
Consumers are shopping around more in search of better deals, Berg said, and booking their tickets earlier to try to lock in reasonable prices.
"Usually I am shouting from the rooftops in the middle of October, 'Book your holiday travel by the end of this month, prices will not go down from here,'" Berg said. "But we actually saw an increase in customers booking holiday travel in September already."
At the airport in Baltimore, some travelers say they're priced out of flying for the holidays this year altogether.
"I'm gonna have to drive," said Rachel Stern of Frederick, Maryland. "I'm from Chicago originally, so I'm gonna drive. For me and my kids, just too much to get tickets."
But others said they're resigned to paying more for their holiday tickets. Mary Haller of Bethany Beach, Delaware is planning a trip to Europe.
"Literally I looked at the economy tickets two weeks ago and they have gone up," Haler said. "It was significant and I sort of had shell shock."
Still, Haller said she has little choice but to buy the tickets anyway.
"I feel bad for people who don't have the means to pay the extra money," she said.

The proposal, which, if finalized, would be the first restrictions on foreign investment in the pharmaceutical industry, prohibits transactions covering "certain bio-derived compounds or materials", biomanufacturing equipment and facilities, and technology related to biological design and sequencing, the Politico reported.

articles.title_orig: Final Israeli polls point to stalemate ahead of Tuesday’s election
articles.title_zh: Final Israeli polls point to stalemate ahead of Tuesday’s election
articles.content_orig:
With no more polls allowed to be released before the election, neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition is reaching the 61-seats necessary for an outright majority
Jack GUEZ / AFP via Getty Images
A road sign stands in front of a large billboard featuring Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (R) of the Likud party and former military chief and leader of the centrist Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on October 20, 2026.
The likeliest outcome of Israel’s upcoming election is a stalemate , according to the final polls ahead of next Tuesday’s election, with neither side — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the bloc opposing him, led by Gadi Eisenkot — projected to reach a majority of the Knesset.
Israeli law prohibits the publication of new polls from Friday until the Oct. 27 election.
The overall polling average put the bloc led by Netanyahu ahead, with 54 seats, while the opposition would get 50 seats, both short of the necessary 61-seat majority. Netanyahu’s Likud polled at 23 seats compared to 21 for Eisenkot’s Yashar party.
However, the gap between polls from right-leaning news outlets and those from the mainstream networks and publications was significant.
In the average of six mainstream TV and newspaper polls, the Eisenkot-led bloc had more seats than the current coalition. An average of polls from the last two days showed Eisenkot’s bloc narrowly ahead, holding 52 seats to the Netanyahu bloc’s 50 seats.
Meanwhile, an average of the polls on Israel’s Channel 14 and i24 News — which rely, respectively, on Shlomo Filber, a former Netanyahu campaign aide, and Direct Polls, the firm Filber founded with former Likud strategist Tzuriel Sharon before departing last year — found Netanyahu’s coalition projected to receive a 61-seat majority of the Knesset, while Eisenkot’s bloc would only have 45 seats. Those polls have been outliers, but Direct Polls was the most accurate in the last election.
The Arab parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, are polling at an average of 14 seats, just short of their record 15 seats in 2020 when they ran together. Leading figures in both blocs have vowed not to include Arab parties in their coalition.
Arab voter turnout has hovered around the 50% mark in the last decade. However, Stat-Net, a polling institute specializing in the Israeli Arab population, has said that it may be as high as 68-69% this year, which may give the parties representing the Arab minority even more seats than projected.
Increased Arab turnout would contribute to higher overall turnout, which would increase the number of votes needed to meet the minimal threshold to enter the Knesset.
In both the general polling average and the right-leaning media’s polls, neither Amcha Yisrael nor the Reservists and Economy Party, which have hovered near the 3.25% electoral threshold in recent weeks, received enough votes to enter the Knesset. In the more left-leaning polls, Reservists and Economy, which has not pledged to recommend either Netanyahu or Eisenkot for prime minister, receives an average of three seats.
An Israel Democracy Institute poll found that Israelis would rather have another election than alternative ways of handling a stalemate. Over a third of Jewish Israelis (35%) and nearly half (46%) of Arabs preferred a repeat election, whereas 28% of Jews and 9% chose a unity government with a rotation for prime minister, and 23% of Jews and 25% chose a minority government.

articles.title_orig: US Treasury proposes a rule to crack down on high-tech investments in China, other adversaries
articles.title_zh: US Treasury proposes a rule to crack down on high-tech investments in China, other adversaries
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Treasury Department is moving to restrict American investment in China’s life sciences industry, releasing long-anticipated proposed rules that add biotechnology to the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (COINS) Act.
Published Thursday, the draft regulations (PDF) categorize “pharmaceutical compounds” as a “prohibited technology” that would trigger an outright ban on certain outbound transactions with “countries of concern,” such as China. The definition of pharmaceutical compounds runs the gamut of different modalities, spanning small molecules, polymers, vaccines, blood products, allergenics, cell and gene therapies, monoclonal antibodies and other recombinant therapeutic proteins, as well as their delivery systems.
If implemented in its current form, the rules would cause additional headaches for U.S. biopharmas looking to tap into China’s biotech innovations. But despite the sweeping scope of the ban covering various types of drug molecules, biopharma business development teams can breathe a measured sigh of relief.
The proposed rule largely spares the regular in-licensing deals and fee-for-service drug R&D collaborations that have driven the majority of muti-billion-dollar deals between Western biopharma companies and their Chinese counterparts. This detail fits the description of a Reuters report in September, which said the Treasury was working on rules that would continue to allow pharma companies to strike most licensing deals for Chinese drugs.
In an accompanying Q&A (PDF), the Treasury Department outlined the types of investment that would be covered under its rules: “Under the proposed rule, certain transactions that involve the acquisition of equity, provision of debt financing that is convertible to equity or that carries certain rights, greenfield investments or other corporate expansions, the creation of joint ventures, or certain LP investments would be covered.
“Activities that do not meet the definition of a covered national security transaction would not be subject to the program except where they are undertaken to evade or avoid the proposed rule,” the agency explained.
Therefore, traditional asset licensing agreements, where Western drugmakers pay cash, milestones and sales royalties for ex-China rights to drugs, fall outside the scope of covered transactions.
The language of the rules matches the current text of the COINS Act itself. COINS was enacted as part of the fiscal year 2026 national defense bill, giving the Treasury the power to scrutinize—or outright prohibit—American investments in sensitive foreign sectors involving countries that it views as adversaries. While the law does not name biotech, it allows Treasury to add new sectors when devising specific rules.
When calls for including biotechnology in the COINS Act emerged earlier this year, Laurie Burlingame, a lawyer at Morse, Barnes-Brown & Pendleton, who specializes in life sciences transactions, explained to Fierce that a pure sectoral expansion of the law likely wouldn’t cover pharma licensing deals, as the law is highly focused on equity investments rather than usual product transactions.
Several high-profile U.S. Big Pharma deals with Chinese companies have drawn scrutiny from Washington’s China hawks in their COINS Act expansion push. But those transactions appear to be pure licensing agreements based on public announcements. These include Bristol Myers Squibb’s potential $15.2 billion deal with Hengrui Pharma covering 13 early-stage programs.
However, some other transaction types that have gained traction lately would fall victim to the rules.
The COINS Act lists “acquisition of an equity interest” in a Chinese entity as a “covered national security transaction.” This provision would prevent U.S. venture capital firms from investing in Chinese biotechs, and it would also impact future deals resembling Pfizer’s recent partnership with 3SBio.
When Pfizer in-licensed a PD-1xVEGF bispecific antibody from 3SBio last year, the New York pharma made a $100 million equity investment in the Chinese biotech. That deal structure would be prohibited under the proposed Treasury rules.
Burlingame previously raised concerns over the COINS Act’s potential impact on the “NewCo” model, in which venture capitalists form a new U.S. biotech based on assets licensed from China. The Chinese licensor often takes an equity stake in the new firm to capture long-term upside.
Under existing COINS language, only a Chinese ownership of 50% or above would make the NewCo a target. But the proposed Treasury rules’ anti-evasion clause could subject any future China NewCo deals that involve an equity interest component to additional scrutiny.
In addition, “entrance into a joint venture” also marks a notable transaction category regulated by the COINS Act.
In its proposed rules, the Treasury deliberately chose not to define “joint venture;” instead, it “refers to the plain English meaning of the term, i.e., as involving the contribution of capital and/or assets by two parties and the sharing of profits and losses.”
This murky definition adds uncertainties to some deals. In Pfizer’s $10.5 billion , 12-asset collaboration with Innovent Biologics, the two companies will co-develop four programs globally and share the development costs, plus U.S. and European profits or losses. Although this unincorporated partnership doesn’t necessarily fit the common idea of a joint venture business, it does involve the contribution of capital from both parties to fund R&D and profit-sharing, and the Treasury said that its term “would not require the establishment or formation of a new entity.”
It’s not immediately clear if the Treasury means to crack down on this deal structure. If it does, the Pfizer-Innovent accord could face regulatory actions—only transactions completed before the enactment of the COINS Act on Dec. 18, 2025 are exempt from the Treasury rules, if implemented.
Following the release of the draft rules, the biopharma industry has reacted with a cautious tone, warning against any broadly restrictive provisions as they study the policy’s details.
“The Administration is correct that biotechnology is a strategic technology industry for the United States. We need policies and initiatives that maintain and advance our global leadership in biotech, particularly as we compete with China,” John Crowley, president and CEO of the influential biotech industry lobby group Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO), said in a statement Thursday.
“The details of the proposed Treasury Department rules matter. We cannot restrict our way to success,” he continued. “As Treasury considers comments on the proposed rule, we need to ensure that we do not have an overly broad approach that would create uncertainty for innovators and investors, and that may unintentionally risk weakening U.S. biotech competitiveness.”
In a separate statement, Kendalle Burlin O’Connell, CEO and president of Massachusetts biotech trade association MassBio, said that “efforts to address national security risks must be carefully targeted to avoid undermining the innovation ecosystem that has made the United States a global leader in developing new medicines.”
“For Massachusetts’ biotech industry, international partnerships and licensing agreements can bring promising scientific discoveries into the U.S. drug development pipeline, where American companies invest in and advance potential new therapies,” she added. “Preserving the ability to develop breakthrough innovations from our own world-leading domestic pipeline while also identifying promising innovations from elsewhere is essential to maintaining America's competitive advantage and access for U.S. patients.”
